findings.why: Water resistance is a tested sun-protection claim that needs a water-resistance test on file and its tested duration stated; neither is on the ad or in the page facts (the cited ISO 24444 test measures SPF only). This sits alongside the 'Sweatproof' hit the rule layer already raised.
findings.fix: Attach the water-resistance test; if it exists, state the tested duration from that report. Otherwise remove 'water-resistant' and keep 'in a lightweight texture'.

findings.span: Meets the EU recommendation of SPF / UVA ratio (3:1)
findings.why: This is a factual compliance claim that depends on a UVA protection test, but the only test cited on the ad is the SPF test; the claim is on the page (F4) without a named source.
findings.fix: Cite the UVA test that shows the ratio in the footnote, or remove the line and keep 'SPF 50, PA++++'.

rule_hit_review.why: 'Sweatproof' is an absolute sun-protection term the rulebook lists as a fail; the page itself advises reapplying after perspiring (F18), which contradicts it. Remove it.

The labelled SPF is stated as SPF 50 and 56 is presented as the in-vivo ISO 24444:2019 test result, which matches the page (F14). The reviewer should confirm that showing the measured value is acceptable.

tone_read: Calm and filter-led: it names the three UV filters and the test standard, with no fear hooks or emoji. It sounds like Minimalist apart from the absolute 'Sweatproof' claim.
language_read: The labelled SPF 50 and PA++++ match the product and the filters are named precisely. 'Sweatproof' and an untested 'water-resistant' overstate what can be claimed; the EU ratio line needs its test source.
